14.1.name: 14.01.md
14.1.text: An overloaded operator is a user-defined operator that changes the "meaning of an operator when applied to operands(s) of a class type". (p. 552) As such, it is a class function, either a member or nonmember, that are meant to perform analogous operations on its operands as the built-in operators. Though, the overloaded version has the same precedence and associativity as the corresponding built-in one (p. 553), because, it is a function, it does not guarantee the order in which operands are evaluated. Therefore, "the comma, address-of, logical AND, and logical OR operators should not be overloaded." (p. 554)

14.4.name: 14.04.md
14.4.text:
```text
(a) %	(b) %=	(c) ++	(d) ->	(e) <<	(f) &&	(g) ==	(h) ()
```

(a) % is a symmetric operator (arithmetic). It should be nonmember function.

(b) %= is compound operator. It ought to be a member function, though is not

```text
required to be so.
```

(c) ++ is an operator that changes its object. It should be a member function.

(d) -> is an operator that changed the state of its object. It should be a

```text
member function.
```

(e) << is a symmetric operator (input or bitwise). It should be a nonmember

```text
function.
```

(f) The logical && should not be overload. (p. 553-554)

(g) == is a symmetric operator (equality). It should be a nonmember function.

(h) The call operator () must be a member function.

14.41.name: 14.41.md
14.41.text: lambdas provide an easier and more concise way to create "disposable" functions on the fly to perform certain tasks, usually one line procedure. They are especially useful when combined with algorithms that take predicates or functions that take pointers to a function or return a function. However, if the task requires procedures that are longer than one line, it is better to use a function-object or a function with std::bind.

14.46.name: 14.46.md
14.46.text: It is not a good idea, because there is not a single one-to-one mapping between Sales_data and the conversions to string or double. For the string type, one could expect the return value to be either a book's isbn or the entire set of data associated with the book (as the name of the class suggests). Should the user require such a conversion, using an explicit conversion operator instead could eliminate the ambiguity. As for the conversion to double, if it would even make sense at all, could lead to surprising results, for it is not clear what value would be returned by the conversion. Thus, it is best not to define one.
